title: Grellin Power: retiring Marsh Creek
prompt: Our client is Grellin Power, a regional utility. Its largest plant, the coal-fired Marsh Creek station, faces two changes at once: new air-quality rules that require a major retrofit to keep operating, and a carbon price coming into force next year. Grellin has publicly pledged to cut its generation emissions by at least 60%. The board must choose between retrofitting Marsh Creek and retiring it — replacing its output with a solar-and-storage build plus market purchases. They have asked us which path to take.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Marsh Creek today, and the retrofit
exhibits.unitsNote: Marsh Creek must keep delivering 5,000 GWh a year in either path; 1 GWh = 1,000 MWh

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — The replacement package
exhibits.unitsNote: The solar-and-storage build and the market contract together replace the full 5,000 GWh

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Annual cost per path, once running

questions.prompt: Before we compare the two paths, what should we clarify with Grellin first? Select the two most relevant.
options: What must each path deliver — how much energy, over what horizon, at what reliability?
Is the 60% emissions pledge a hard constraint on this decision, or an aspiration?
Which architect designed the Marsh Creek turbine hall?
How many followers does Grellin have on social media?
What was Marsh Creek’s construction cost in the 1970s?

optionRationale: The two paths are only comparable if they deliver the same thing; “replace” must be defined before it can be costed.
A must-have. If the pledge binds, a cheaper high-emission path is not actually available, and the option set shrinks.
Architectural history does not bear on the decision.
Sunk cost — what the plant cost to build says nothing about what to do with it now.
commonMistakes: Comparing costs before fixing what each path must deliver
Treating the public pledge as marketing rather than asking whether it constrains the answer

questions.followUp:
Both paths must deliver Marsh Creek’s full 5,000 GWh a year at utility reliability — the storage in the replacement package is sized for that, and the market contract is firm.

And the pledge binds: the board will not approve a path that leaves the 60% reduction out of reach. Cost decides between paths that comply.

questions.prompt: Which areas would you investigate to choose between retrofit and replacement? Select the four most relevant.
options: The full cost of keeping Marsh Creek — retrofit, running costs, and the new carbon price
The full cost of the replacement — build cost, running costs, and market purchases
The emissions outcome of each path against the 60% pledge
The paint scheme of the new solar farm
Risks of each path — construction delay, market price exposure, and the plant workforce

optionRationale: One side of the ledger — and the carbon price is new, so yesterday’s cost picture is already wrong.
The other side of the ledger, including the energy the package buys rather than builds.
The binding constraint: a path that fails the pledge is out regardless of cost.
Real on both sides: a big build can slip, market purchases float with prices, and a coal closure lands on real jobs.
Not relevant to a generation decision.
Historical prices are not what the plant will pay.
commonMistakes: Costing the retrofit path at today’s costs and forgetting the carbon price starts next year
Leaving the workforce and community impact out of a coal-closure structure

questions.followUp: Here is Marsh Creek’s cost position, including the carbon price that arrives next year. Work from these figures.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what will it cost to run Marsh Creek for a year once the carbon price is in force — fuel, operations and carbon together?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Fuel and O&M: 5,000 GWh = 5,000,000 MWh × $40 = $200M a year.
Emissions: 5,000,000 MWh × 0.9 t = 4.5 Mt a year.
Carbon: 4.5M t × $20 = $90M a year.
Total: $200M + $90M = $290M a year.
commonMistakes: Leaving the carbon cost out — it is the new fact that changes the plant’s economics
Slipping a factor of 1,000 between GWh and MWh
Adding the retrofit here; it is a one-off, not a running cost

questions.followUp: So keeping the plant costs $290M a year before the retrofit is even paid — $90M of it is the carbon bill on 4.5 Mt of emissions, a line item that did not exist last year.

questions.prompt: What is the total five-year cost of the retrofit path — keeping Marsh Creek compliant and running?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Running cost: $290M × 5 = $1,450M.
Plus the one-off retrofit: $1,450M + $600M = $2,050M.
commonMistakes: Charging the $600M retrofit every year
Using the pre-carbon running cost of $200M
Forgetting the retrofit entirely — without it the plant cannot legally run

questions.followUp: Just over $2B to keep the old plant alive for five years. Now cost the alternative. Here is the replacement package.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what does the replacement package cost per year, once built — solar operations plus market purchases?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Solar O&M: 3,000,000 MWh × $10 = $30M a year.
Market purchases: 2,000,000 MWh × $50 = $100M a year.
Total: $30M + $100M = $130M a year.
commonMistakes: Pricing all 5,000 GWh at the market rate
Forgetting the purchased energy and costing only the solar half
Mixing the $/MWh figures across the two components

questions.followUp: Right: $130M a year against $290M for coal — a $160M annual gap in the replacement’s favour once it is running, as the chart shows. The question is whether that gap earns back the much larger build cost.

questions.prompt: What is the total five-year cost of the replace path, including the build?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Running cost: $130M × 5 = $650M.
Plus the one-off build: $650M + $1,200M = $1,850M.
commonMistakes: Adding the retrofit cost to this path — retiring the plant is how it is avoided
Charging the build cost per year
Comparing builds only ($1,200M vs $600M) and concluding retrofit is cheaper

questions.followUp: So replacement costs $1,850M against $2,050M for the retrofit — $200M cheaper over five years, despite the build being twice the retrofit. The running-cost gap does the work. Cost favours retirement; now check it against the pledge.

questions.prompt: Using the emissions figures in Exhibits 1 and 2, by what percentage does the replace path cut Marsh Creek’s emissions?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number — for 75%, type 75.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Coal today: 4.5 Mt a year.
Replace path: solar is zero-carbon; market purchases 2,000,000 MWh × 0.45 t = 0.9 Mt a year.
Reduction: (4.5 − 0.9) / 4.5 = 80%.
commonMistakes: Calling the replace path zero-emission and answering 100% — the purchased power carries the grid’s carbon
Computing the cut on energy (60% solar share) instead of on emissions
Reporting what remains (20%) instead of the reduction

questions.followUp: An 80% cut, well past the 60% pledge — and the cheaper path as well. Before recommending a coal closure, though, the board will ask about everything the spreadsheet leaves out.

questions.prompt: What are the most relevant risks of retiring Marsh Creek and building the replacement? Select the three most relevant.
options: Construction risk — the solar and storage build arriving late or over budget while the coal plant has already committed to closing
Market price risk — 2,000 GWh a year bought at prices that float
Workforce and community risk — the plant’s jobs and the town around them
Coal marketing risk — customers preferring coal-fired electricity
Logo redesign risk after the transition

optionRationale: The classic energy-transition trap: sequencing. Retire before the replacement is proven and the utility is short 5,000 GWh.
Real: $100M a year of the case is bought at $50/MWh, a number the market sets, not Grellin.
Real and central to a just transition: several hundred jobs and a local economy sit on this decision, and regulators and politicians will weigh it.
Electricity is fungible; customers cannot tell and by and large prefer cheaper and cleaner.
commonMistakes: Sequencing risk missed — treating retirement and build as independent events
Costing the transition while ignoring the people in it

questions.followUp:
Construction: keep Marsh Creek’s closure date contingent on the replacement’s commissioning tests, not the calendar.

Market exposure: contract most of the 2,000 GWh forward, and revisit expanding storage later.

Workforce: fund retraining and redeployment into the build and operations of the new assets, and engage the town early — a contested closure is a slow closure.

questions.prompt: Grellin’s board chair asks for your recommendation on Marsh Creek. Please give your answer in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the recommendation: retire Marsh Creek and build the replacement
Gives the cost case with numbers: $1,850M versus $2,050M over five years — $200M cheaper despite the larger build
Explains why: the carbon price turns the old plant’s $290M running cost into the expensive option
Gives the pledge answer: an 80% emissions cut against the 60% commitment
Names the conditions: closure tied to commissioning of the new assets, forward contracts on the purchased power, and a funded workforce transition
Stays inside seven or eight lines
commonMistakes: Comparing the two one-off costs and recommending the retrofit
Presenting the closure as purely financial and omitting the workforce plan
Claiming the replacement is zero-carbon when a fifth of the emissions remain via market power

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
